'''Fiber functors''' in [[category theory]], [[topology]] and [[algebraic geometry]] refer to several loosely related [[functor|functors]] that generalise the functors taking a [[covering space]] <math>\pi\colon X\rightarrow S</math> to the ''fiber'' <math>\pi^{-1}(s)</math> over a point <math>s\in S</math>.

== Definition ==
A '''fiber functor''' (or '''fibre functor''') is a loose concept which has multiple definitions depending on the formalism considered. One of the main initial motivations for fiber functors comes from [[Topos theory]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=SGA 4 Exp IV|url=http://www.normalesup.org/~forgogozo/SGA4/04/04.pdf|last=Grothendieck|first=Alexander|date=|website=|pages=46–54|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200501174937/http://www.normalesup.org/~forgogozo/SGA4/04/04.pdf|archive-date=2020-05-01|access-date=}}</ref> Recall a topos is the category of sheaves over a site. If a site is just a single object, as with a point, then the topos of the point is equivalent to the [[category of sets]], <math>\mathfrak{Set}</math>. If we have the topos of sheaves on a topological space <math>X</math>, denoted <math>\mathfrak{T}(X)</math>, then to give a point <math>a</math> in <math>X</math> is equivalent to defining adjoint functors<blockquote><math>a^*:\mathfrak{T}(X)\leftrightarrows \mathfrak{Set}:a_*</math></blockquote>The functor <math>a^*</math> sends a sheaf <math>\mathfrak{F}</math> on <math>X</math> to its fiber over the point <math>a</math>; that is, its stalk.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2001-38-04/S0273-0979-01-00913-2/S0273-0979-01-00913-2.pdf|title=A Mad Day's Work: From Grothendieck to Connes and Kontsevich – The Evolution of Concepts of Space and Symmetry|last=Cartier|first=Pierre|author-link=Pierre Cartier (mathematician)|date=|website=|page=400 (12 in pdf)|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405212545/https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2001-38-04/S0273-0979-01-00913-2/S0273-0979-01-00913-2.pdf|archive-date=5 Apr 2020|access-date=}}</ref>

=== From covering spaces ===
Consider the category of covering spaces over a topological space <math>X</math>, denoted <math>\mathfrak{Cov}(X)</math>. Then, from a point <math>x \in X</math> there is a fiber functor<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.renyi.hu/~szamuely/heid.pdf|title=Heidelberg Lectures on Fundamental Groups|last=Szamuely|date=|website=|page=2|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405211320/https://www.renyi.hu/~szamuely/heid.pdf|archive-date=5 Apr 2020|access-date=}}</ref><blockquote><math>\text{Fib}_x: \mathfrak{Cov}(X) \to \mathfrak{Set}</math></blockquote>sending a covering space <math>\pi:Y \to X</math> to the fiber <math>\pi^{-1}(x)</math>. This functor has automorphisms coming from <math>\pi_1(X,x)</math> since the [[fundamental group]] acts on covering spaces on a topological space <math>X</math>. In particular, it acts on the set <math>\pi^{-1}(x) \subset Y</math>. In fact, the only automorphisms of <math>\text{Fib}_x</math> come from <math>\pi_1(X,x)</math>.

==== With étale topologies ====
There is an algebraic analogue of covering spaces coming from the [[étale topology]] on a connected scheme <math>S</math>. The underlying site consists of finite étale covers, which are finite<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~dcorwin/files/etale.pdf|title=Galois Groups and Fundamental Groups|last=|first=|date=|website=|pages=15–16|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200406003039/https://math.berkeley.edu/~dcorwin/files/etale.pdf|archive-date=6 Apr 2020|access-date=}}</ref><ref>Which is required to ensure the étale map <math>X \to S</math> is surjective, otherwise open subschemes of <math>S</math> could be included.</ref> [[Flat morphism|flat]] surjective morphisms <math>X \to S</math> such that the fiber over every geometric point <math>s \in S</math> is the spectrum of a finite étale <math>\kappa(s)</math>-algebra. For a fixed geometric point <math>\overline{s}:\text{Spec}(\Omega) \to S</math>, consider the geometric fiber <math>X\times_S\text{Spec}(\Omega)</math> and let <math>\text{Fib}_{\overline{s}}(X)</math> be the underlying set of <math>\Omega</math>-points. Then,<blockquote><math>\text{Fib}_{\overline{s}}: \mathfrak{Fet}_S \to \mathfrak{Sets}</math></blockquote>is a fiber functor where <math>\mathfrak{Fet}_S</math> is the topos from the finite étale topology on <math>S</math>. In fact, it is a theorem of Grothendieck that the automorphisms of <math>\text{Fib}_{\overline{s}}</math> form a [[profinite group]], denoted <math>\pi_1(S,\overline{s})</math>, and induce a [[continuous group action]] on these finite fiber sets, giving an equivalence between covers and the finite sets with such actions.

=== From Tannakian categories ===
Another class of fiber functors come from cohomological realizations of motives in algebraic geometry. For example, the [[De Rham cohomology]] functor <math>H_{dR}</math> sends a motive <math>M(X)</math> to its underlying de-Rham cohomology groups <math>H_{dR}^*(X)</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jmilne.org/math/xnotes/tc.pdf|title=Tannakian Categories|last1=Deligne|last2=Milne|date=|website=|page=58|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref>
